26 In one of the first experiments to demonstrate the Doppler effect, a train was filled with trumpeters
all playing a note of frequency 440 Hz. The difference in observed frequency of the note as the
train directly approached a stationary observer was 22 Hz. The speed of sound was 340 m s–1.
At which speed was the train moving?
A
15.4 m s–1
B
16.2 m s–1
C
17.0 m s–1
D
17.9 m s–1

hints: Notice the train is directly approaching, so the observed frequency is higher: $f_o = 440 + 22 = 462 \text{Hz}$, not $440 \text{Hz}$.
Connect this to the moving-source rule: approach shortens the effective wavelength to $(v - v_s)/f_s$, so $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$.
Rearrange to $v - v_s = v f_s / f_o$ and then solve $v_s = v - v f_s/f_o$ using $v = 340 \text{m s}^{-1}$, $f_s = 440 \text{Hz}$ and $f_o = 462 \text{Hz}$.
walkthrough: Identify the useful data: source frequency $f_s = 440 \text{Hz}$, increase $\Delta f = 22 \text{Hz}$, so observed frequency $f_o = 462 \text{Hz}$, and wave speed $v = 340 \text{m s}^{-1}$.
State the Doppler rule for a source moving directly toward a stationary observer: $f_o = f_s \times v/(v - v_s)$, where $v_s$ is the train speed.
Rearrange for the train speed: $v - v_s = v f_s / f_o$, so $v_s = v - v f_s / f_o = v(1 - f_s/f_o)$.
Calculate the intermediate result: $22/462 \approx 0.04762$, so $v_s \approx 340 \times 0.04762 \approx 16.2 \text{m s}^{-1}$ with a unit check of $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
This is option B, while using $22/440$ gives the $17.0 \text{m s}^{-1}$ approximation that neglects the change in denominator.

A.explanation: Gives $15.4 \text{m s}^{-1}$, which is too small and does not satisfy $f_o = f_s v/(v - v_s)$ with $f_o = 462 \text{Hz}$.

B.explanation: Gives $16.2 \text{m s}^{-1}$, which satisfies the approaching-source equation for $440 \text{Hz}$ shifted by $22 \text{Hz}$ with $v = 340 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

C.explanation: Gives $17.0 \text{m s}^{-1}$ from the approximation $v_s \approx v \Delta f / f_s$, which ignores that the denominator must use the observed $462 \text{Hz}$.

D.explanation: Gives $17.9 \text{m s}^{-1}$, which is too large and predicts an observed frequency greater than $440 + 22 = 462 \text{Hz}$.
